verdict.reasoning: Patient: “I was having a bit of chest discomfort… felt not exactly a pain, but like a pressure on my chest. Feels like someone's sitting on my chest.”
Patient: “I was doing some gardening couple of hours ago, and I felt not exactly a pain, but like a pressure on my chest.” This indicates onset a couple of hours ago during gardening.

Patient: “It's in the middle of my chest… not necessarily to one side. And it's quite a diffuse pain.” and “mainly my left arm… and in my shoulder as well.” Supports central, diffuse pain radiating to left arm/shoulder.

Activity: “it started just when I was gardening… I was just kneeling down… wasn't during any physical exercise.” First occurrence: Doctor: “Have you had this before?” Patient: “No, this is the first time, actually.”
Patient: “I've noticed a bit of nausea, not. No vomiting…” clearly indicates nausea without vomiting.
Patient: “I'm pretty sweaty” indicates diaphoresis.
Patient: “pretty sweaty, short of breath” confirms associated shortness of breath.

Patient: “Yeah, it's beating a bit faster now. I think that's because I'm a little bit stressed… but I haven't noticed it beating faster than usual.” He denies palpitations beyond stress; fact states he reports palpitations with discomfort.
Same episode description: “I'm pretty sweaty, short of breath” during the chest discomfort supports being diaphoretic and short of breath during the episode.
Doctor: “Now do you have these symptoms right now or have they gone off now?” Patient: “No, they're still present.” and “you've still got the chest discomfort right now? – Yes.”
Doctor: “Do you have high blood pressure or high cholesterol or diabetes?” Patient: “Yeah, I have high blood pressure but not diabetes.”
Patient: “Yes, actually I have an allergy to aspirin… it's an allergic reaction… I swallow a bit, but nothing life threatening… It's a mild reaction to it.”
Patient: “So my father died of a heart attack…” and age: Doctor: “Can you remember what age roughly he was…?” Patient: “He was about my age.” Doctor clarifies “Around 60?” Patient: “Around 60, yes.”
Patient: “my father died of a heart attack and my mother had some heart problems.”
Patient: “Yeah, I smoke a fair bit. So I smoke about 10 cigarettes a day… For the past 15 years.”
Alcohol: Patient: “I drink per week? Probably about seven or eight pints a week… Oh, beer, yes.”
Doctor: “I can't tell from the video. Are you overweight?” Patient: “Yes, I'm overweight, yeah.”
Doctor: “Do you normally live alone?” Patient: “Yeah, I live alone at the moment. Yeah, it's just me in the house.”
Work: Patient: “I work as a restaurant owner. So I own a sushi shop.”
Doctor: “And how much activity do you do normally? Do you walk a lot or do you run…?” Patient: “No, I don't. I generally don't do much activity at all.”

Doctor: “The symptoms that you've described to me, they indicate the possibility of a heart attack… our number one priority to exclude that.” Combined with ongoing central chest pain and risk factors (smoking, HTN, family history, overweight) supports concern for ACS/MI.
Hypertension as a problem is supported by history: Patient: “Yeah, I have high blood pressure…” Using it as an assessment is a direct clinical inference from documented past medical history.

Aspirin allergy and mild reaction are discussed in detail and explicitly highlighted as important: “It's very important that you communicate that to the hospital… because we may need to consider aspirin despite.” Treating it as an assessment is a reasonable clinical inference.

Transcript documents smoking (10/day for 15 years), alcohol intake (7–8 pints/week), and overweight, all known cardiovascular risk factors. Describing them as contributors to cardiovascular risk is a direct clinical inference from these social history details.
Doctor: “We're probably gonna have to call an ambulance for you.” and later references ambulance coming due to concern for heart attack, aligning with suspicion for acute coronary syndrome.
Doctor: “ambulance team will be with you very shortly. I'm going to stay on the line with you until they come, okay?”
Doctor: “When they come, what they'll do is they're going to put some stickers on your chest and do an ECG and then decide where to take you after that.”

Doctor: “It's very important that you communicate that to the hospital detail you've just told me because we may need to consider aspirin despite.” While not explicitly saying the doctor will convey it, the plan to ensure the hospital receives this aspirin allergy detail is clear.

Doctor: “team will assess you and then they may take you in to one hospital or another… Once they come, then I'll hand over to them. I'll explain what's going on.” This implies handing over the history and risk factors and transferring care to EMS.

Doctor: “We're probably gonna have to call an ambulance for you.” and “ambulance team will be with you very shortly… they're going to put some stickers on your chest and do an ECG and then decide where to take you after that.”
Patient self-reports “I'm pretty sweaty,” but there is no objective physical examination or clinician statement confirming observed diaphoresis.
Patient self-reports “short of breath,” but the transcript does not document an objective assessment by the clinician of observed dyspnea.

Fact states subjective tachycardia; patient downplays this: “Yeah, it's beating a bit faster now. I think that's because I'm a little bit stressed… but I haven't noticed it beating faster than usual.” He attributes it to stress and denies noticing it faster than usual overall.
Doctor: “In the house with you at the moment?” Patient: “No, no one's in the house at the moment.” and “Is your front door open? – Yes, it's open.” Confirms he is alone and front door is open.
